comments.author: Jono Bell
comments.comment: The big gap I still see is observability, not capability. Once an agent can take long-running actions, you need traces, rollback points, permissions, and evals the same way you need tests for production code. Otherwise “autonomous” just means harder to debug.

comments.author: Mahdi Rashidi
comments.comment:
AI usually removes tasks before it removes accountability.

The big shift I see is that “I can code” becomes less valuable than “I can define the right problem, verify the output, and own the edge cases.” Cheap agents make prototypes easy, but production still punishes vague specs, weak evals, and missing judgment.

comments.author: Tony Drummond
comments.comment:
10 parallel agents sounds productive until review becomes the bottleneck.

The pattern I’ve seen work best is giving each session a tiny spec, a clean branch, and a pass/fail check it can run without asking you. Otherwise you don’t get 10 builders, you get 10 streams of context debt.

comments.author: Steve Goldsby
comments.comment: The real moat is the eval harness plus routing policy, not the checkpoint. Once you can replay tasks, score regressions, and swap models behind the same tool/memory layer, local vs hosted becomes an infra decision instead of a religion.
